With the latter type, the shape of the seal normally corresponds to the motif itself (7g. 4./—7). Anthropomorphic subjects are most often shown on round seals with an open back; thus, more rarely than on zoomorphic seals do anthropomorphic depictions dictate the shape of the seal.*” Represented are hybrid or mythical creatures, bird-headed or winged “gods” and “demons” which are sometimes seated upon mounts. Naturalistic representations are rather exceptional.” In particular, connections can be drawn between the first-mentioned group and representations of the second millennium BC from the Syro-Mesopotamian and Elamite world.”! The use of compartmented seals as stamps is attested by imprints on clay from Shahr-e Sokhta and-Shahdad,” but such evidence is rare in Turkmenistan and Bactria: a few sealings are published from Gonur south, Djarkutan, and Altyn Depe.” Some specimens were found near the pelvis in tombs of the Namazga V Period in Altyn Depe. This may indicate that the seals were carried on a ribbon and buried with the dead (Masson 1988: 89). In Margiana, Sapalli Depe and Djarkutan they were offered exclusively at female burials.”* The context of seals from illegal excavations in Bactria is not known, but most likely many of them were burial gifts as well. Recently, Parpola (2005a) has pointed out that impressions on clay tablets from Mohenjodaro were made with metal compartmented seals (fig. 3.5—6; the seals used are different from the two fragments discussed below). This important observation not only enlarges the corpus of exotic objects, but also provides further evidence for the use of these seals as stamps. 5. xxxiv UTE FRANKE The compartmented seal, which likely measured about 5.5 cm in diameter, has a closed back and an outer ring of small ovoid cells of which six are still visible. In the interior, two small leaf-shaped cells on either side of a longer, curvilinear cell can still be discerned. The two small cells attached to it towards the centre appear to be more shallow. The outer fringe of the central cell is just preserved, but it cannot be determined whether a geometrical ornament or a figural depiction was shown there. Although the simple rosette is a common motif, the number of petals depicted normally varies between four and ten. Numerous examples are known from Damin,'°’ Shahr-e Sokhta I,’ Tepe Qandar (fig. 3.8),'° Altyn Depe'TM and Bactria (fig. 3.9-10).'°° The assumption that the central portion of the seal was occupied by a figurative motif is supported by a comparable piece from Bactria (fig. 3.2).'° It features an outer ring of 21 cells, an arrangement that could also be reconstructed for the seal from Mohenjo-daro.'”’ An eagle in heraldic pose with spread wings and head turned to the side occupies the centre of the seal. This motif is among the most common of the animal depictions displayed on compartmented seals. xxxvi UTE FRANKE Stylistically, this piece of high quality and elaborated details stands out from among other metal compartmented seals. In any case, the number of seals of this type is limited: a few examples are known from Altyn Depe, Sarazm, Margiana, and Bactria.'*° Apart from the eagle and very few human figures, goats and bulls are depicted, but a clear distinction between the latter two is not always possible. The example from Altyn Depe that is described by Sarianidi as “humped bull with Indus influence” could likewise represent a goat judging from its short tail and missing horns, but for the little hump-shaped pendant (?) on the back (fig. 4.4).'° Also, the identity of a “prey” is unclear (fig. 4. 7).'*7 Animal heads are shown either in profile or en face. Examples of either a goat or a bull motif, preserved in fragments only,'”* and a bull seal!”’ from Altyn Depe are both distinguished by a single round and centrally located eye, as visible on the seal from Mohenjo-daro. Technically as well as stylistically, these examples are closely related to another seal from Nausharo that clearly depicts a humped bull (fig. 4.2). Due to its find spot on the surface, Jarrige (1986: 85, pl. XX XIX:b) attributed the seal to Nausharo IB, or around 2700/2600 Bc. While this date corresponds with the appearance of compartmented seals in the Indo-Iranian borderlands,'*° in the north the time range of this small zoomorphic group of seals is rather related to the late Namazga V or Kelleli phase. A corresponding horizon was later also uncovered at Nausharo (Period IV) and Dauda Damb,” ' and is well documented in the surrounding area at Sibri, Mehrgarh VIII and Quetta.’ As far as style is concerned, a gold pendant from the Quetta hoard is amongst the best comparisons for the seal from Mohenjo-daro.’*? Both seals can be regarded as imports to Mohenjo-daro. Their location and associated objects indicate that they come from the urban context, even though from its late or latest phase. Stylistic and contextual data indicate a slightly later date for seal no. 1 than for no. 2, the “bull seal”. The late Namazga V comparisons from Altyn Depe and from the Quetta hoard point to a date within the last two centuries of

The third phase, comprising the first centuries of the second millennium BC, is characterized by the consolidation and expansion of the BMAC and the localization process in the Indus region, marked by the appearance of small, rather rural communities, such as, e.g., Pirak, post-urban ; Harappa, and the Jbukar horizon.'** The two compartmented seals from Mohenjo-daro belong to the second phase. While the animal-shaped “bull seal” (no. 2) might — like the eagle seal from Harappa — belong to an older tradition and reflect the increasing significance of Margiana, the find spots of both seals belong to late urban contexts. Therefore, although they do not contribute to the discussion about the development of that style, their presence is important evidence for long distance interaction at a time when Margiana was emerging as a new centre. Inscribed Objects from Harappa Excavations 1986-2007 J. MARK KENOYER RICHARD H. MEADOW Introduction Ever since the discovery of the first engraved seals of the Indus Civilization at the site of Harappa, scholars have been trying to unlock the secrets of the Indus script’ and to understand the social, economic, and political importance of these and other inscribed objects. Although the inscriptions have remained undeciphered, it has been possible to gain some insight into the context for the use of the script based on carefully documented recovery of inscribed objects from recent excavations throughout the greater Indus region. In this volume, we present for the first time in one place the assemblage of inscribed and incised objects discovered at the site of Harappa during excavations conducted between 1986-2007 by the Harappa Archaeological Research Project (HARP)’. ' That “writing” and “script” are appropriate terms to employ in reference to what has commonly been called the “Indus script” has been contested by Farmer, Sproat and Witzel (2004). They argue that the Indus script is not likely to have been linked directly to a spoken language and was probably a system of non-linguistic symbols. We, however, contend that given the development in the system of inscriptions over time as seen at Harappa and given the extensive use of the “signs” or “symbols” both formally and informally and on many media (see text discussion), making the distinction between a language-based script and a not-so-tied-to-language symboling system is not a particularly interesting distinction. In any event, in the absence of multi-lingual texts, long texts, and/or a successor symboling system or script, there can be no widely accepted understanding of what the symbols or signs of the “Indus script” actually meant to those who employed them, and thus there can be no true resolution of this issue. As a result, we continue to employ terms like “script” and even “writing” in their broadest senses and are well aware that not everyone may agree with such usage. We are also rather imprecise in our use of the terms “inscribed” and “inscription”, which we employ broadly in relation to the Indus script and not in the restricted sense of something engraved, incised, or written. Thus pieces with script in relief are also referred to as inscribed (although not “incised”).

Finally the term “tablet” is used in the sense employed in all volumes of the Corpus of Indus Signs and Inscriptions to refer to small inscribed pieces specially made of stone, terracotta, faience, or copper — with images and/or script incised or in relief — that are not intaglio seals. * The Harappa Archaeological Research Project (HARP), a long-term program of investigations into the origins and character of Indus urban centers, was first initiated at Harappa by the late Prof. George F. Dales and Dr. J. Mark Kenoyer (Dales & Kenoyer 1993). In 1992, the original University of California-Berkeley project was transformed into the Harappa Archaeological Research Project directed by Dr. Richard H. Meadow (Harvard University) and Dr. J. Mark Kenoyer (University of Wisconsin-Madison), Co-Directors, and Dr. Rita P. Wright (New York University), Assistant Director. In the catalog presented in this volume, to the degree of specificity possible given the current state of analysis,° we have assigned a chronological period to an inscribed object based on the stratigraphic and associated artifact information from its find spot. When an inscribed object has been recovered from redeposited sediment, it often can be associated with a particular period based on its material, style, carving technique, iconography, etc. For example, Ravi or Early Harappan pottery with graffiti’ that has been found in mixed context can be identified based on the nature of the ceramic ware, shape, and/or decoration and assigned to the period for which those ceramic features are characteristic. With seals this is more difficult, particularly with geometric or button seals. One example is the specimen H-1537 that was originally assigned to Period 2. After layout of the plates for this volume was completed, microscopic analysis of the tool marks on the inscribed surface and comparison with seals from secure contexts suggests that this seal actually is probably from Period 3C. Another object (H-1539) that we initially thought to have been intentionally marked is a lump of low fired-clay that bears multiple incised parallel lines. Re-examination has revealed that these lines may in fact be the result of markings made by a small animal (perhaps a bird or rodent) and not the result of intentional human modification. General Site Chronology and Highlights of the Excavations Beginning as a small village that was established ca. 3700 BC on an elevated river terrace between the Ravi and the old Beas Rivers, the ancient settlement we today designate as Harappa grew to become a small town with two major walled areas by ca. 2600 BC. Over the next 700 years during the Harappa Phase, ca. 2600-1900 BC, the city expanded with the construction of several walled suburbs and extra-mural occupation areas, covering an area of more than 100 and perhaps as much as 150 hectares (Meadow & Kenoyer 2005). The Early Harappan periods The Ravi Phase represents the initial occupation of the site (Period 1: ca. 3700 — ca. 2800 BC) and has cultural similarities with early settled communities in the Ghaggar-Hakra River valley to the east, as well as in many small regional cultures in the piedmont and highlands of Baluchistan to the west. Evidence from the analysis and sourcing of the raw materials used for chipped-stone and ground-stone manufacture, bead making, and shell bangle production indicate that the site was linked to distant resource areas throughout the Indus region (Kenoyer & Meadow 2000). There is also evidence to suggest strong trade links to regions north of See the Bibliography. Other crafts such as bone working, pottery making, and mud-brick architecture construction were also evolving during this early occupation as was the use of pre-firing “potter’s marks” and post-firing “graffiti” on pottery, indicating that concepts of graphic expression using abstract symbols were emerging (Kenoyer & Meadow 2000). Over time, the economic and political importance of this small community resulted in its growth and expansion during the Kot Diji (Early Harappa) Phase (Period 2: ca. 2800-2600 BC). During this period, Harappa became a large settlement, possibly a regional center, integrating its hinterland and obtaining raw materials from new resource areas (Kenoyer 1997), although an emphasis on northern resources continued to be important (Law 2005; 2008). The use of pre-firing potters’ marks and post-firing graffiti on pottery became more widespread, with clear evidence for the use of multiple signs that continued to occur and evolve through the Harappa Phase (Period 3). These, we believe, represent an Early Indus symboling system or script that had become clearly differentiated from potters’ marks (Kenoyer & Meadow 1996; 1999; Kenoyer 2006). Furthermore, it was during this phase that standardized cuboid stone weights, terracotta tags impressed by inscribed seals, and steatite seals with animal and geometric motifs came to be employed. The Harappan periods Although many urban characteristics of Harappa began during the Kot Diji Phase, it was in the following Harappa Phase (Period 3: ca. 2600-1900 BC) that the settlement became a major urban center, expanding on previously established links to other areas of the greater Indus Valley and beyond (Meadow & Kenoyer 1997). With the rise of the Indus cities, technology and craft production increased in sophistication and scale of production. The use of what seems to be a relatively standardized form of the core Indus script became more common, being employed on seals as well as on a wide range of other artifacts including tablets, tools, ornaments, and various types of pottery. The signs and symbols were carved, incised, chiseled, inlaid, painted, molded, and embossed on a variety of (preserved) materials including terracotta, ceramic, stoneware, and glazed faience; shell, bone, and ivory; sandstone, steatite, and gypsum; copper and copper alloys, silver and gold. While the use of signs on Indus seals is fairly well studied, until recently there have been no systematic studies of their use on other kinds of objects due to the small numbers of such objects or their fragmentary nature. These different kinds of inscribed artifacts are now being studied spatially and chronologically and compared with seals from similar contexts and periods. Although we are still only at the beginning of this study, it seems that signs on seals and tablets usually reflect a more formal use of the script while those on other artifacts may be more informal and even, in some cases, represent the more spontaneous use of various signs. Spontaneity is particularly likely for graffiti on ceramic vessels, which were incised with script after manufacturing and firing. This use of signs clearly demonstrates that it was not only craftsmen commissioned to prepare formal devices who incised the script, but also others who employed it directly to label a container with perhaps one or more of the following: the name of its owner, the nature of its contents, its origin, its destination, or an incantation — to name some of the more obvious possibilities. Regrettably, most examples of ceramic vessels with incised signs are broken, with the inscription only partially preserved on the recovered sherd(s). ee Inscribed Objects from Harappa Excavations 1986-2007 xix This provides a challenge in trying to investigate what degree of overlap there may be in sign sequences between graffiti and inscriptions on seals, tablets, or other media. Much of our recent work at Harappa has focused on understanding the details of cultural developments during Periods 3B and 3C. Results reveal these to have been dynamic periods of urban expansion together with recurrent decay, rebuilding, and reorganization in different parts of the city. our recent work at Harappa has focused on understanding the details of cultural developments during Periods 3B and 3C. Results reveal these to have been dynamic periods of urban expansion together with recurrent decay, rebuilding, and reorganization in different parts of the city. In 2000 and 2001, excavations turned to recovering more information on Period 3A in order to reveal initial Harappa Phase developments, particularly relating to the use of inscribed pieces. This period is poorly represented in excavations at most Indus sites, because the remains are buried under later occupation levels. At Harappa, it has been possible to recover two seal fragments from Period 3A, providing an important baseline against which to evaluate stylistic and technological change in the use of seals (see below for more discussion). Based on evidence at hand to date, square seals with script together with the unicorn or other animal motifs are associated primarily with the Tater part of Period 3A and are relatively common throughout Period 3B and on into Period 3C (Meadow & Kenoyer 1997). Square seals with script alone are found first in Period 3B, but long rectangular seals with script alone are confined to Period 3C. We are also obtaining important chronological information with respect to inscribed tablets, which are particularly common at Harappa, more so than the seals. Through careful stratigraphic cutting-back of Vats’ section in Trench I of Mound F and comparison with his report of that trench (Vats 1940), we have determined that he was not correct in reporting that small steatite tablets with incised script are from the earliest levels of the site. Instead it is evident that such tablets appeared toward the middle of Period 3B and continued to be used well into Period 3C (Meadow & Kenoyer 1997; 2000). Furthermore, these inscribed steatite tablets, which Vats (1940) called “tiny steatite seals”, are not seals at all but are incised with script that was to be read directly from the tablet. And along with the steatite tablets are found terracotta and glazed faience tablets with molded bas-relief script, motifs, and narrative scenes, which also start appearing in mid-Period 3B and continue into Period 3C (Meadow & Kenoyer 1997; 2000). And along with the steatite tablets are found terracotta and glazed faience tablets with molded bas-relief script, motifs, and narrative scenes, which also start appearing in mid-Period 3B and continue into Period 3C (Meadow & Kenoyer 1997; 2000). While many of the tablets are rectangular in form, others were made in circular, half circle, or fan shapes and even in the form of trees, fish, hares, or other animals. Most tablets are flat in cross-section, but others are triangular, deeply rectangular to square, plano-convex, biconvex, or almost cylindrical (e.g., this volume: H-1956 & H-1957 and H-1979, H-1980 & H1981). This last form has led to much confusion in the literature as they are often incorrectly referred to as cylinder seals. So far, no true cylinder seals have been recovered from the HARP excavations, although the Central Asian type of cylinder seal is reported from earlier excavations and from other sites (Parpola 1994). Unlike seals, almost all of which are unique, an important aspect of tablets is that, at Harappa (as well as at Mohenjo-daro), there are numerous instances of (1) incised steatite tablets with copies of the same signs and/or motifs and (2) duplicate bas-relief tablets of faience or terracotta made from the same mold (e.g., Meadow & Kenoyer 2000). Other copies and duplicates have been found scattered across the site where, like the multiples above, they are always found in trash, fill, or street deposits. Why tablets were made, how they were used, and why they were discarded remain intriguing unanswered questions. Their intrinsic interest lies not only in the script that they often bear, but even more so in the iconography, which provides an important glimpse, however fragmentary, into details of Harappan ideology, particularly for the time frame from ca. 2400 to ca. 2000 BC (Harappa Period 3B through much of Period 3C). For a more detailed discussion see Meadow & Kenoyer 2000. Two other forms of inscription that should be mentioned are (1) impressions stamped (originally) on soft clay used to seal a container (pot, box, room, etc.) and (2) imprints stamped on a ceramic vessel before firing. Very few of the first have been recovered from Harappa, or indeed from any Indus site with the notable exception of Lothal where 93 specimens were retrieved clustered mostly in the area of a structure termed a “warehouse” by the excavator (see Frenez & Tosi 2005 for a review of this material). From the HARP excavations, only six sealings or “tags” have been identified (H-1719 through H-1724), all of which were partially hardened through low firing, possibly in a hearth, hot ashes, or rubbish fire. Due to the secondary contexts of the sealings, it is not possible to determine if the hardening was done intentionally as a way to archive a sealing or unintentionally as a part of post-deposition processes. A seventh impression in the form of a sub-conical “jar-stopper” (H-1725), however, was recovered in completely unbaked condition. Only immediate intervention by HARP object conservators was able to keep this specimen from disintegrating because of crystallization of the salts in the raw clay upon drying. At Harappa as at Lothal, it was the at-least-lightlybaked condition of the tag fragments that permitted them to be recovered intact. Unbaked specimens that are not immediately recognized as impressed are likely not to be preserved at many Indus sites, which may go some way toward explaining why such seal impressions have rarely been recovered in the Indus area. More common than seal impressions on tags are imprints with script on ceramic vessels that were stamped before firing. These are found almost exclusively on those Harappa Period 3C vessels called “pointed base goblets” or PBGs (see H-1081 and H-1082 for nearly complete and complete examples). To judge from the quantities of sherds recovered at Harappa, such vessels were mass-produced in the tens if not hundreds of thousands. A very small percentage of the PBG vessel fragments recovered by HARP bear impressed stamps with one or more signs (H-1727 to H-1766). The seals used to make these imprints are of the long rectangular form found only in Period 3C, just as PBGs are also found only in that chronological period (ca. 2200-1900 BC). Six sherds of PBGs with identical stamped imprints as those herein illustrated as H-1756 to H-1759 have also been recovered from the site of Lahoma Lal Tibba located ca. 24 km ESE of Harappa (Wright 2009, fig. 5.11). These provide strong evidence for the distribution of ceramics between Harappa and smaller settlements in its hinterland. Inscribed Objects from Harappa Excavations 1986-2007 li The Late Harappan period(s) The Late Harappan or Cemetery H levels at Harappa date from approximately 1900-1700 BC (based on HARP excavations and radiocarbon dates), although the Cemetery H occupation may continue to as late as 1300 BC or even 1000 BC based on excavations in other parts of the greater Indus region (Kenoyer 2005). Early and mid-twentieth century excavations of material from this time period at Harappa were concentrated in the cemetery area south of Mound AB extending east along the southern edge of Mound E. Very few preserved habitation areas remain due to the extensive brick robbing of the upper levels of the site. However, some areas with partial structures and in situ floors have been discovered, revealing the use of smaller-size fired bricks that, however, still maintain the traditional Harappan height:breadth:length ratio of approximately 1:2:4. Other discoveries relate to crafts such as pottery making and to faience, glazed, and stone bead production. These Late Harappan domestic structures and associated floors have provided valuable information about the nature of early second millennium BC subsistence, architecture, and everyday life. Instead of having been abandoned, the settlement appears to have been thriving, albeit much reduced in size, and it remained part of important cultural, economic, and ideological transformations. However, there is no indication of the use of inscribed seals, or indeed of formalized inscriptions of any kind, during this period. Some Late Harappan ceramics have post-firing graffiti, but the abstract symbols do not represent a continuation of the Indus script system as has been argued for sites such as Lothal (Rao 1991). These recent discoveries by HARP at Harappa indicate that there were significant changes in the style of the script and also in the types of objects on which Indus signs were executed during the emergence, expansion, and transformation of the Indus cities. In other words, the Indus script did not appear fully formed and remain unchanged for more than 700 years. Seal Carving — Chronological Changes in Technology and Style No seals of types that later came to be characteristic of the Indus Civilization have been recovered from the earliest Ravi Phase occupation at Harappa. That said, there is a single fragment of a bone seal with a perforation near the center (H-1521), the design of which was carved deep into the soft inner portion of the bone, leaving the hard outer surface in relief. Because of slight burning and weathering, it is difficult to know if this button seal was used to stamp anything or was only used as an ornament. Carved intaglio seals and seal-impressed clay are first seen at Harappa during the Early Harappan, Kot Diji Phase (Period 2: ca. 2800-2600 BC). One unfired and unfinished steatite intaglio seal fragment (H-1533) was found in a well-defined sealed stratum that can be securely dated to that phase based on ceramic associations. This broken seal has a roughly incised elephant that was probably only partly completed before the seal broke. The boss on the back is missing, but traces of a drill hole indicate that the seal had such a boss before it was damaged. The blank for this seal seems to have been sawn from a larger blocklet of steatite

The seal has a relatively simple geometric design of four intersecting lines that create eight triangular sectors on the seal. The edges and surface of the seal are smoothed and rounded, but there are numerous manufacturing or grinding striae that are still visible. The seal may have been used to impress clay or some other material, and the perforated boss on the back may have been used to hold a cord. Harappa Phase Carved Seals Only two seals, both incomplete, have been recovered from the lowest levels of the Harappa Phase (Period 3A). One example (H-1688) is a broken steatite seal from street deposits on Mound E, dating to ca. 2600 BC. (Kenoyer 1991; Dales, Kenoyer et al. 1991, fig. 13.44e). The style of carving is bold and angular, consisting of a single sign above the rump of a bovine, which, to judge by comparison with a complete seal from the site of Farmana in Haryana, might be a water buffalo (Shinde et al. 2008: 104, fig. 107). The deeply carved V-shaped sign or symbol has not been found on any later seal, but a rounder and more symmetrical form does occur on molded tablets. The animals carved on later seals also are more naturalistic with smooth contours that reflect the actual muscles of the animal. The second Period 3A seal fragment from Harappa (H-1689) comes from a deposit on the western edge of Mound E that was found to contain both Early Harappan and Harappan pottery. This seal has an elephant motif with naturalistic lines and may represent the development of seal carving styles at the end of Period 3A or the beginning of Period 3B. Further welldated examples are needed to clarify the earliest style of seal carving, but these two seal fragments from Harappa, and the examples from Farmana, suggest that styles of carving seals evolved over time and that some of the signs also changed over time.

Our excavations have recovered unfinished and finished seals from contexts some of which can be accurately dated and associated with specific activity areas at Harappa. Unfinished seals have been recovered from across the site, and through detailed comparisons, it may be possible to identify specific workshop styles and changes in carving techniques. One of the unfinished unicorn seals (H-1683), a fragment of which was found on the northeastern slope of Mound E, has such a distinctive style of carving used for the ritual stand — as well as for the unicorn’s collar, ear, and horn — that it should be readily identifiable on finished seals. Indeed, a comparable carving style is seen on a finished unicorn seal (H-1682) from a Period 3B context in a nearby trench on the eastern edge of Mound E some distance from where the unfinished seal was found. Silicone impressions have been taken of all seals with well-preserved surfaces, and finegrained molds from these can be used to make high-resolution photographs with a scanning electron microscope (Kenoyer 1997; 2003). This technique provides the means to identify distinctive features of tool marks and cutting angles, which then can be compared between seals. Such a process can lead to the definition of tool types and even to identification of specific tools and special features of carving technique, all of which can assist us to understand the

liv J. MARK KENOYER & RICHARD H. MEADOW nature, development and even the organization of seal-carving traditions. Already we can suggest, based on the recovery of unfinished seals with only the animal motif present, that this part of the seal was carved first, followed by the script. Going further, using the evidence provided by detailed characterizations of carving style and technique, it may be possible to determine if one artisan carved animal motifs while another artisan specialized in carving the script. In the end, it may also be possible to define specific workshops and even individual artisans.'° - One rare example of a seal without any animal motif (H-1692) was recovered in a dustbin outside of a house at the northeastern edge of Mound E. The house associated with this structure can be dated to Period 3B, and this seal may represent an early example of what was to become the long rectangular seal with script (e.g. H-1704 to H-1715) that became quite common in subsequent Period 3C. This early example, however, is only slightly longer than it is wide and has the grooved boss typical of seals with animal motifs. Examples of similar types of seals have been reported from Mohenjo-daro (CISI 1, p. 78: M-313, M-316, M-315) and Lothal (CISI 1, p. 251: L-56, L-58, L-59), but for those sites the context and dating of such seals are not well understood. Based on the stratigraphic and chronological contexts of seals found from Harappa, there appears to be significant changes in the types of boss used during different periods and on different types of seals. lvi J. MARK KENOYER & RICHARD H. MEADOW Conclusions When both seal carving styles and boss types are considered together, there is good evidence for an evolution in seal forms over time. Whether there were parallel changes in the script needs to be investigated in detail. In the past, studies of the Indus script have lumped all of the best-preserved seal inscriptions together and used this combined assemblage as the basis for a study of the script. Based on the discoveries at Harappa, it is now possible for that site at least to separate out different chronological periods of seal production and to compare seal inscriptions with those found on other types of objects such as incised and molded tablets and pottery, which together greatly outnumber the seals and seal impressions recovered from the site. The use of Indus signs on distinctive types of objects as well as upon ornaments and pottery indicates common cultural practice at sites of the Indus Civilization. This shared practice may be a reflection of or have played a role in the integration of populations within and between urban centers as well as with communities spread out across rural areas, along trade routes, and in resource areas. Especially as new excavations produce stratigraphically controlled and well-dated inscribed pieces, it becomes both possible and increasingly important that the script and accompanying iconography be subjected to rigorous analysis at the site, regional, and cross-regional levels to investigate trends of change through time and variability across space. When such studies have been carried out, assumptions about the uniformity of the signing system (Parpola 1994) probably will need to be revised. Even though these new discoveries will not lead to a decipherment of the Indus script, any new patterns that can be discerned at Harappa and at other sites where close stratigraphic and spatial documentation has been possible, will help us to better interpret the role of the script in the Indus world. In our opinion, too much scholarly (and lay) emphasis has been placed on the unattainable goal of decipherment of the Indus script and not enough on treating seals, tablets, and other inscribed materials as archaeological finds that went through processes of materials selection, production, use, and discard. New Light on “Major Clark”, Owner of the First Published Indus Seal ASKO PARPOLA Alexander Cunningham’s report (1875) of his visits to Harappa initiates our knowledge of the Indus Civilization. It contains the first site plan of Harappa and drawings of some Indus antiquities. The most curious object discovered at Harapa is a seal, belonging to Major Clark, which was found along with two small objects like chess pawns ... (Cunningham 1975: 108); this is all we know of the provenance of this “stone seal”, of which Cunningham’s drawing (1875: pl. 33, fig. 1, reproduced above) misleadingly shows not the actual face, but its impression (see H-1048). Gregory Possehl has tried to trace the personal history of all people connected with the discovery of the Indus Civilization, but in this case is forced to speak of “a man known only as ‘Major Clark’” (Possehl 1999: 52). J. R. Fleet (1912) published a photograph of an impression and

shows not the actual face, but its impression (see H-1048). Gregory Possehl has tried to trace the personal history of all people connected with the discovery of the Indus Civilization, but in this case is forced to speak of “a man known only as ‘Major Clark’” (Possehl 1999: 52). J. R. Fleet (1912) published a photograph of an impression and reported that the seal was presented to the British Museum by “Major (General) Clark”. On this basis, Nayanjot Lahiri, another scholar who recently has been at pains to trace the discovery history of the Indus Civilization in detail, writes: Hardly anything can be gleaned about Clark or his career in the army, other than that he procured the Harappa seal before 1872-73 [when Cunningham last visited Harappa], and that he was Major General Clark by the time he presented it to the premier museum of his native land (Lahiri 2005: 28). In the British Museum, the seal has the accession number 1892-12-10, 1, and is recorded as having been “Given by Maj. Gen. M. G. Clerk, 1892”. In British English, Clerk is pronounced like Clark, so both Cunningham and Fleet apparently have just heard the name and misspelt it. Clerk’s full name is Malcolm George Clerk, and he was born in 1836. This information can be found in library catalogues recording a book published in 1895 by this author, who according to the title page was Major-General. Entitled Catalogue of the coins of the Achaean league, the booklet deals with Greek numismatics, a hobby explaining Clerk’s interest in the seal from Harappa.

According to the internet archive of the Families in British India Society (FIBIS), Clerk applied for cadetship in the East India Company Armies in 1853-54, was Lieutenant in the Bengal Army (regiment: late 4th Europeans) in 1863, and married Marietta Forest in Bengal Presidency in 1866. Official records published by G. W. Forrest reveal that Clerk participated in suppressing the Sepoy Mutiny as an artillery officer. The message sent on the 8th of January 1858 by Major V. Eyre, commanding Artillery Brigade of the Bengal Army in Alumbagh, near Lucknow, ends as follows: Lieutenant D. Gordon, who had assisted me most zealously in working the heavy guns in actions of Mungulwar and Alumbagh, was left behind at the latter place in command of a portion of the heavy battery, as also Lieutenant G. it passed to Mr M. Longworth Dames and from him to the British Museum on the 7th of March 1912, Clerk’s seal had been given to the British Museum by its owner as early as 10th December 1892. After Harvey, too, had done the same on the 29th of June 1912, J. F. Fleet published an account and the first photographs of all three. The paper drew the attention of Sir John Marshall to these curious finds, which eventually led him to initiate the excavations at Harappa. They thus play a vital role in the discovery of the Indus Civilization. These seals are naturally discussed by Gregory Possehl (1999: 52) and by Nayanjot Lahiri (2005: 28-29) in their praiseworthy accounts of how the Indus Civilization was found. Both however make the same mistake by assuming that all these three seals are contained in a photographic plate of three seals in the British Museum, which Possehl (1999: pl. 2.4) and Lahiri (2005: fig. 6) published in illustration. This plate, however, does not contain O'Connor's seal (H-1021) but instead a seal from Mohenjo-daro (M-1765) transferred from India to the British Museum on the 16th of April 1947. The FC numbers for the objects coming from Mohenjo-daro and Harappa are for the most part keyed to the illustration aumbers in the plates of the excavation reports, and largely serve also as abbreviated references to these basic publications (1 is prefixed to the numbers of MIC, 2 to those of FEM and 3 to those of EH); though there are some differences, a similar reference system was adopted by I, Mahadevan in his book The Indus script (New Delhi 1977). Objects from the old excavations of Mohenjo-daro and Harappa not illustrated in the excavation reports have, for the most part, FC numbers starting with 0 (for Mohenjo-daro) and 37— 39 or 4 (for Harappa). Column 3 gives the excavation numbers or corresponding data. The abbreviations appearing in the excavation numbers are not included in the following list of abbreviations. For the excavation mumbers of Mohenjo-daro, consult Franke-Vogt 1991; for those of Harappa, see EH, the separate introduction to H-1521 to H-2583 on p. 430, and the introductory essay on the HARP material by J. K. Kenoyer and R. H. Meadow in this volume (pp. xliv—Ivill). Column 4 mentions the museum where the object is [or was] kept or its owner, with the museum registration number(s). Registration numbers put into square brackets refer to objects not found in the museums where they are supposed to be. The Harappans had a unique script of their own, and thousands of short inscriptions have survived, but the script vanished when the Indus Civilization collapsed. So far there is no such key as the Rosetta Stone, which opened up the secrets of the hieroglyphic writing. This does not mean that it is impossible to gain some understanding of the Indus script, but this demands proper research methods. A serious study of the Indus script requires access to all available material in good images. More than half of the Indus texts have been carved on small stone seals, which usually have some iconographic motif in addition to the text. Normally an animal is depicted very realistically, but there are also for instance anthropomorphic figures probably representing divinities. Indeed, these small seals are our principal sources of Harappan art and religion. The find places of the seals, their material and methods of manufacture, also contribute to the knowledge about Harappan administration, trade routes and crafts. Incised or painted graffiti, including singly occurring “potter’s marks”, form another major inscriptional category. Corpus of Indus Seals and Inscriptions (CISI) aims to publish, in high quality images and as completely as possible, the seals and inscriptions associated with the Indus Civilization. Volume 1: Collections in India, was produced in collaboration with the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) in 1987, and Volume 2: Collections in Pakistan, in collaboration with the Department of Archaeology and Museums, Government of Pakistan (DAMGP) in 1991. A third volume (New material, untraced objects, and collections outside India and Pakistan) started being prepared in the 1990s. It was soon realised that a single book could not contain all the material that remained to be published. The sites

The sites of Mohenjo-daro and Harappa have produced the great maj ority of the known Indus seals and inscriptions, but many objects excavated in the 1920s and 1930s were not to be found in the museum collections published in CISI 1-2. Still, photographs of lost objects could be recovered by carefully sifting the photo archives of the ASL Besides, much new material came from the fresh excavations of the Harappa Archaeological Research Project (1986-2007). Volume 3, Part 1: Supplement to Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, was brought out in collaboration with the HARP directors J. M. Kenoyer and R. M. Meadow in 2010. Sites with more abundant seal and graffiti material were selected for the present volume, to ease the demand for space in the final volume with a large number of sites. Mehrgarh, Nausharo, Sibri and Dauda-damb in Pakistani Baluchistan were excavated under the direction of Jean-Francois (+) and Catherine Jarrige from 1974 until 2002. Jyrki Lyytikka photographed the seals from these sites in Karachi in 1986 for their inclusion in CISI, and subsequently Catherine Jarrige supplied her own photos of the missing items, along with photographs of the seals excavated by Jean-Marie Casal in 1951-58 at Mundigak in southeastern Afghanistan. While many seals from Mundigak have probably been kept unpublished in the Kabul Museum, some are housed at Musée Guimet in Paris and photographed by Catherine Jarrige. Héléne Tromparent, who wrote her Master’s thesis on the seals of Mehrgarh, Nausharo, Sibri and Dauda-damb, was entrusted with writing the introductory essay to this material published in this volume and to

vill Preface prepare a preliminary catalogue of the data. Thanks are due also to Gonzague Quivron for permission to reprint here his splendid study of the Mehrgarh and Nausharo graffiti. The excavations of Mehrgarh, Nausharo and Sibri along with their analytical interpretation by J.-F. Jarrige and his team have created a firm basis for understanding cultural evolution in the Indo-Iranian borderlands, and provided a continuous archaeological sequence from the Neolithic to the Iron Age. With regard to the origins of the Indus Civilization, one must also mention the publication of J.-M. Casal’s excavations (1962-65) at Nindowari along with a documentation of the Kulli culture ceramics coming from recently looted graveyards (J.-F. Jarrige et al. 2011). In their conclusion, J.-F. Jarrige and his colleagues emphasize that the Kulli culture had already fully developed by 2600 BCE, before the formation of the Indus Civilization between 2600 and 2500 BCE. The Kulli culture also retained its separate identity in southern Baluchistan until 1900 BCE. The animal iconography of the Kulli pots goes back to earlier local traditions and includes as one of its important motifs “bull tied to a kind of post or tree”. The scene greatly resembles the most important iconographic motif of the Indus seals, the “unicorn” bull standing in front of a peculiar stand. Bulls tethered to fig trees are a prominent motif also at Nausharo I D, immediately preceding the Harappan Period Nausharo II. Evidently the roots of the Indus Civilization are in the earlier cultures of the Indo-Iranian borderlands, which in turn are connected with the cultures of the eastern half of the Iranian Plateau and southern Central Asia. This wide area remained an interaction sphere even in Harappan times (Lamberg-Karlovsky & Tosi 1973; Cortesi et al. 2008; J.-F. Jarrige et al. 2011), when it was — as in later times — the departure area for new immigrations to the Indus Valley (J.-F. Jarrige & Quivron 2008). In order to understand better the formation process of the Indus Civilization and the background of its seals, including foreign seals found in Harappan contexts, it seems necessary to widen the scope of CISI to include also seals discovered in archaeological excavations of prehistoric eastern Iranian Plateau and southern Central Asia (excluding the great multitude of seals that come from looted

order to understand better the formation process of the Indus Civilization and the background of its seals, including foreign seals found in Harappan contexts, it seems necessary to widen the scope of CISI to include also seals discovered in archaeological excavations of prehistoric eastern Iranian Plateau and southern Central Asia (excluding the great multitude of seals that come from looted graves of these regions). An important site, with seals closely related to those of Mundigak and Mehrgarh, is Shahr-i Sokhta, the capital of the “Helmand Civilization” of ancient Seistan. Massimo Vidale and Alessandra Lazzari, who participated in the excavations of Shahr-i Sokhta and are in charge of the excavation archives, immediately agreed to my proposal to collect the published glyptic material from Shahr-i Sokhta and include it in this volume. They also wrote an introductory essay and sent me relevant publications not accessible in Helsinki. Period I at Shahr-i Sokhta, dated to the early third millennium BCE, witnesses the presence of Proto-Elamites at the site, using Mesopotamian-type cylinder seals, while the local ceramics are related to the Damb-Sadaat/Quetta Ware distributed right to the borders of the Indus Valley. Shahr-i Sokhta was the easternmost point of the Uruk Expansion until Roland Besenval (2011: 49-51 & 133, figs. 121-122) brought to light typically Proto-Elamite bevel-rimmed vessels at Mir-i Qalat in Pakistani Baluchistan. The cylinder seals disappear after Period I, and Period II at Shahr-i Sokhta starts with the introduction of stone and metal seals and related ceramics, apparently coming from southern Turkmenistan (Geoksyur I / Namazga III). As many seals and sealings from Shahr-i Sokhta have not been assigned to definite periods, the material has been arranged typologically. The site of Chanhu-daro, in lower Sindh, was excavated by Ernest Mackay in 1935-36 (CE, 1943). Most of the finds remained in India, and the seals from Chanhu-daro in the care of the ASI were published in CISI 1. Many seals and other objects, however, could be taken to the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (BMFA), which had been financing the excavation. Possehl was no more there to write an introduction to the Rojdi section of this volume; therefore a more extensive discussion of the excavations of this site is in order. Rojdi is the name of the largest “Sorath Harappan” site situated right in the centre of the Saurashtran Peninsula. A small trial excavation was conducted there by P. P. Pandya in 1957-58. This excavation produced the first and so far the only certain Mature Harappan Indus inscription found at Rojdi (Rjd-2; in Rjd-3 only the initial sign remains, but it is also likely to be an Indus inscription). It was published right away in IAR 1957-58 along with some graffiti. The Gujarat State Department of Archaeology continued excavations at Rojdi in 1958-59 and 1964-65, but the results remained unpublished save for brief reports in the respective volumes of IAR. The fourth and fifth seasons of excavation in 1982-83 and 1983-84 were conducted in collaboration by two teams of archaeologists, one led by Gregory L. Possehl of the University of Pennsylvania and a Gujarati team led by Y. M. Chitalwala. A very substantial report of these excavations (practically just the fourth season), Harappan Civilization and Rojdi by Gregory L. Possehl and M. H. Raval (Director of the Gujarat State Department of Archaeology), was published in 1989. The contributions by five team members include a thorough analysis of the Sorath Harappan ceramics by Frank Herman (pp. 53-156). Herman’s paper includes figure 65 with drawings of twenty “Graffiti from Rojdi”, with their data detailed in the text portion. These 20 graffiti, however, do not include those graffiti that have been published in the numerous other figures illustrating the shapes and other details of the vessels recovered at Rojdi. Publishing the Rojdi material with the excavation seasons as the main sorting criterion follows Possehl’s practice, and is particularly suited for the graffiti, for with few exceptions mentioned below they are all from the last, Post-Urban, or Late Sorath Harappan period Rojdi C (dated to c. 1900— 1700 BCE). The two earlier periods, Rojdi A (c. 2500-2200 BCE) and Rojdi B (c. 2200-1900 BCE), fall within the period of the Indus Civilization, but differ materially from the “classical Indus Civilization”, which is represented at several other sites in Gujarat by what Possehl has called “Sindhi Harappans”, i.e. Harappans who came to Kutch and elsewhere in Gujarat from Sindh c. 2500-2300 BCE. Rojdi with its 7.5 hectares is the largest site of what Possehl has called “Sorath Harappans”, a poorer regional variety of the Saurashtran Peninsula. (Possehl 2002: 82-88.) When the reinvestigation of Rojdi began, it was noted that the pottery of Rojdi was clearly of the Harappan tradition, but it lacked the key Urban Phase Harappan ceramic markers: for example, the goblet, beaker, ‘S’ form jar ... and the tea cup with a perforated handle. It is also true that Rojdi has not yielded a single sherd with the Indus black on red painting style. The site has also failed to produce any of the Harappan stamp seals or the other Urban Phase Sindh Harappan paraphernalia of daily life as found at sites such as Mohenj o-daro ... (HCR, p. 11.) Also conspicuous by their absence in any phase are signs of industrial and manufacturing activity at Rojdi. There are no furnaces, kilns, wasters or slag. ... Thus, if we look at Rojdi, with its houses, compounds, and food-producing and storage facilities, its overall character suggests a farmer’s village. ... the Harappans of Saurashtra were part of the larger cultural mosaic we now call the Indus Civilization, but they had their own ‘flavor’ and unique characteristics. At present, however, all the finds excavated by the Italian Mission (MAI) at Shahr-i Sokhta and given to the Italian partner are kept, together with the whole collection of the former Museo Nazionale d’Arte Orientale “Giuseppe Tucci”, in the store rooms of the Museo delle Civilta (MuCiv, Rome). Unfortunately, we are informed that at present the objects are not yet fully accessible for study, but they undoubtedly will be in the near future. As a first step towards the publication of the Shahr-i Sokhta seal corpus, we decided to accept Asko Parpola’s proposal to include in the present volume all the seals and sealings that have been published so far (with more or less satisfactory standards) in the main field reports or specific papers. A substantial further collection of unpublished seals and sealings is planned to appear in the last volume of the CISI series. We take the opportunity of summarizing in this short note some of the main topics and reasons of interest of this important class of finds. General Issues The large early urban site of Shahr-i Sokhta, in the first half of the 3rd millennium BC, appeared as a dense cluster of private dwellings looking out into a haphazard network of dusty alleys. As life thrived and the city grew, large dumps were piled up in vacant lots, while sediments spilled over floors and living surfaces. This required a constant process of rebuilding, in which pavements were raised with fills largely made of ceramics, while roofs were rebuilt at a higher level on top of each room. For these reasons, although some erections (particularly those destroyed by a wide-scale destructive event at the end of Period I) were sealed in contexts of primary firing and collapse, Period II buildings are entirely filled with secondary layers and fillings, and it is quite problematic to refer artifacts, among them seals and sealings, to their primary architectural and functional associations (unbaked clay sealings in this regard are better evidence, because of their ephemeral and fragile materiality). This dynamic process of stratigraphic formation,

in contexts of primary firing and collapse, Period II buildings are entirely filled with secondary layers and fillings, and it is quite problematic to refer artifacts, among them seals and sealings, to their primary architectural and functional associations (unbaked clay sealings in this regard are better evidence, because of their ephemeral and fragile materiality). This dynamic process of stratigraphic formation, with the likely chance that older seals came to be included in younger deposits, and the evidence in other sites of re-use of old seals centuries later,” makes the chronological definition of many seals quite uncertain. How far this implies female property and administrative functions, it is hard to say. A random sample of 75 reasonably stratified seals from the settlement (roughly speaking, more than 10% of the total) shows some clear trends. Cylinder seals are almost regularly found in Period I contexts; copper alloy seals appear at the end of Period I, and in Period II account for about 11% of the total. Stamps made of relatively soft stones (like chlorite and limestone, more rarely lapis lazuli) form 80% of the Period II specimens, the rest (9%) being bone and shell seals, which seem to be a specific choice of the same Period. In the following Period III, 71% of the seals are compartmented stamps in (leaded) copper alloy, while the remaining 29% are made in stone. Period IV witnesses the use of smaller and quite simple stamps, made of terracotta. The strong increase of copper stamp seals from Period II to Period III was probably linked to major societal changes. In Period III, large portions of the urban space were taken up and expropriated by wide architectural complexes, like the two buildings united by a threefold wall, including inner partitions, of the Central Quarters (Salvatori & Vidale 1997), occupying a rectangular area of c. 80 x 45 m. Other large houses probably of the same Period had a similar pattern (large rectangular courtyards surrounded by rows of cells, with major residential buildings at one end) (Moradi & Sajjadi 2012). The sudden disruption of rules of inheritance and management of urban spaces is obvious. At this point, while the manufacture and replacement of the older stone stamps required the contribution of specialized providers and stone cutters who maintained exclusive links with the relative source areas, the shift to cast copper stamps allowed urban dwellers to produce their own seals with the same base material — in itself a widely accepted form of circulating wealth. Moreover, a copper stamp seal, to a certain extent, could be reproduced at will using its impression as a mould;? reproducibility of stamp seals might have been an added advantage when a trading family had to expand rapidly

French Archaeological Mission at the Sites of Mehrgarh, Nausharo, Sibri and Dauda-damb (Kachi District, Balochistan, Pakistan) and at Mundigak (Afghanistan) HELENE TROMPARENT All the seals and seal impressions unearthed in Balochistan by the French Archaeological Mission under the direction of Dr Jean-Francois Jarrige between 1975 and 1996 have not been published exhaustively so far, although some of the objects have already appeared in various publications.’ The seals and seal impressions found at Mundigak (Afghanistan) by the team led by Jean-Marie Casal between 1951 and 1958 were only very partially published.* Most of the objects from Mundigak have been kept in the Kabul Museum since their discovery, but their present location there is uncertain, due to the political troubles and lootings in Afghanistan since 1979. In accordance to an agreement between the French and Afghan governments, some of the objects have been kept in the Musée Guimet in Paris until now. Only 21 of the Mundigak seals are found in the Musée Guimet, mainly those that were photographed by J.-M. Casal. For six of these, the period to which they belong in the chronology of the site is still uncertain. As a matter of fact, a lot of work is still needed on the archives in order to establish the context of those which have never been published. All the seals coming from the above-mentioned sites are being studied by the author of this short essay.’ The seals from Nausharo will appear with an analysis in the final publication of the excavation results. XVili HELENE TROMPARENT _ There are three main periods identified in the general continuous sequence of Mehrgarh / Sibri / Nausharo: PreHarappan, Mature Harappan and Late Harappan. The term “Early Harappan” was used to label Period VII of Mehrgarh and Period I of Nausharo in CISI 2. But to speak of an “Early Harappan” phase of the times immediately preceding the Indus Civilization is confusing. Even if Period VII of Mehrgarh and Period I of Nausharo present characteristics which announce the Indus Civilization, especially in the ceramic production, the said period is clearly not part of the Indus Civilization. The more general term “Pre-Harappan’”, applicable to all periods from the beginnings until just before the Indus Civilization, has been favoured here. The dates given in the chart below are broad. They are based upon stratigraphy and radiocarbon dating of samples taken in all areas of the sites. In 1997, the excavation of the Neolithic settlements and cemeteries of Mehrgarh was resumed, and the chronology of the Neolithic has been slightly revised. A period called I C, represented only by tombs in the excavated area, was added to the general chronology (J.-F. Jarrige et al. 2013). Incised and Painted Marks on the Pottery of Mehrgarh and Nausharo-Baluchistan GONZAGUE QUIVRON [This paper was first published in: Raymond Allchin & Bridget Allchin (eds.), South Asian Archaeology 1995, I: 45-62. Cambridge: The Ancient India and Iran Trust, 1997. ] The Sites The sites of Mehrgarh and Nausharo are known to have been centres of intensive pottery production. During the preIndus period, in the second half of the fourth and the first half of the third millennium, this industry went through a dynamic stage of development leading toward a kind of mass production. In the chronological framework of the two settlements this sequence corresponds to Mehrgarh Periods [V-V—-VI and VII A-B—C (3600-2700 BC) (C. Jarrige et al. 1995) and Nausharo Period IT A-B—C—D (2900-2500 BC) (J.-F. Jarrige et al., in press). During those periods, the sites were found to be particularly rich in remains of potter’s activities. Rooms were used for storage of hundreds of vessels, sometimes found stored in baskets or in jars. Unfired pottery and potter’s tools were also found in great numbers. Associated with the buildings were also many remains of kilns as well as pottery wasters. Many pre-firing incised marks have been observed on the pottery manufactured at both sites during those periods, on utilitarian unpainted ware as well as sometimes on high quality painted ware. The following Periods II and III of Nausharo correspond to the Indus Phases (second half of the third millennium). Numerous remains of potter’s activities such as workshops and kilns were also uncovered in the levels of these periods. Most of the marks found on pottery are graffiti scratched after firing. But, as during the pre-Indus period, pre-firing incised marks still occur, although much less frequently. These enigmatic pre-firing markings which most probably represent a system of intelligible symbols were in existence for many centuries (Quivron 1981). Many possible uses have been ascribed in publications and the idea that these signs were forerunners of the Indus script has also often been expressed. But, so far their significance is not understood. Comparison with Other Sites and Relationship of the Signs with the Indus Script The size of the collection from Mehrgarh and Nausharo is large, but not unique. Incised marks were found on vessels from many other sites. They were in existence over a vast area for many centuries, and attest to considerable continuity in the tradition of incising signs on vessels. They were used as early as the fifth millennium in Elam at sites such as Djowi and Djaffarabad (Dollfus and Encrevé 1982) and were still used in the second millennium in Margiana and Bactria for example at Togolok and Dashli (Hiebert 1994). Their greatest use was however during the fourth and mainly the first half of the third millennium. Figures 5 and 6 illustrate the parallels between the Mehrgarh and Nausharo marks corpus and those of other sites. A high degree of similarity can be traced with sites in Baluchistan, in the Quetta Valley (Fairservis 1958), but many marks are also common with Rehman-Dheri (Durrani et al. 1994-95) or Sarai Khola (Halim 1972), with Shahr-i Sokhta in Seistan or with Mundigak (Casal 1961), Tepe Yahia (Potts 1981) and other sites’. 1 Casal 1964; Dales 1979; Fairservis 1959; 1976; Hakemi 1976; Khan 1965; Lal 1960; 1992; Rao 1963. Incised and Painted Marks on the Pottery of Mehrgarh and Nausharo-Baluchistan XXV Many symbols are common to the various sites.2 But this visible similarity of signs is most probably due to the use, in each corpus, of a range of simple geometric designs which are also comparable with many symbols occurring in elaborate writing systems. Many signs have parallels in the proto-Elamite script ( fig. 1, sign no. 82 and fig. 2, signs no. 20, 21, 22, 28, 34, A1, 43 and 45) as well as with many basic signs of the Indus script (Parpola 1994). The relationship between the two writing systems has often been suggested by the possibility of a link through the pre-Indus incised marks on pottery (Potts 1981).2 But many comparable marks from Susiana or Mehrgarh IV are dated earlier than the creation of the proto-Elamite system and similar pre-firing marks were still incised on vessels at a time when the Indus script was already known. This continuity of use of pre-firing marks, although much less frequently, seems to argue against the hypothesis that the roots of the Indus script are in the incised marks tradition of some predecessors. The simple designs of the comparable pre-existing signs, easily produced by a tool or a stylus, may be the reason why they were adopted, intentionally or not, in the Indus script. The pre-firing marks are always single signs and the assumption that they may have been part or variants of even a crude form of writing cannot be proved, but they probably represent a system of mutually intelligible symbols commonly accepted through time and space, and it seems likely that these incised marks were merely utilitarian. Significance of the Symbols: New Elements Furnished by the Excavated Sites Among the different possible interpretations, the marks are sometimes described as representing goods which might be contained in the vessels or indicated their capacity. A number of Mesopotamian pots bear inscriptions indicating their capacity, particularly the large jars. At Mehrgarh, the great majority of incised pots are small goblets and plates which are not shape types of vessels made to conserve goods. As for the capacity, 21 different sign types have been recorded on the side or underside of bases of hundreds of almost identical goblets and in many other cases, the same symbol was incised on vessels of different shapes and sizes. It is also difficult sometimes to analyse the incised marks from various sites because many of them were found on potsherds or on vessels not always assigned to particular periods or areas. This is not the case at Mehrgarh and Nausharo where numerous groups of complete incised pots were found in structures linked to potter’s workshops. A dense accumulation of jars mostly identical in form was uncovered in the levels of Period VI. This structure is an open firing of superimposed layers of clay jars in which the bulk of the vessels was abandoned due to a failure of the firing process (Audouze & Jarrige 1979). Many jars in this structure were used as firing containers or saggars in a phase of the manufacturing cycle. A semifluid mixture of clay and straw covered the external surface of their rims, probably to stick a lid on, and one of them was even entirely covered with this coat of clay. The purpose of these jars was to protect objects or vases from breakage as well as from combustion gas and flames in a reducing atmosphere. This technique, known at Mehrgarh at the end of the fourth millennium, was also used later at Mohenjo-daro where a group of coated jars was uncovered. The mouth of one of them was sealed with the classic unicorn seal. There was no sealing on the coating of the jars from Mehrgarh but several of them were incised with marks either on the rim or on the

Distribution of Sign Types through Time Figure 9 shows the distribution of sign types through time at Mehrgarh and Nausharo from the middle of the fourth to the middle of the third millennium.> The marks are dominant in Period VII (2900-2700 BC). Almost all the sign types of the corpus are used during this period and many exclusively during it. Some signs (fig. 2, sign no. 29) incised on pottery in early periods disappear in course of time. Some others (fig. 2, signs no. 32 and 45) also from early periods, are not used for a long time and appear again in more recent periods, and a few sign types (fig. 2, sign no. 40) occur only during the more recent periods. There is a more or less temporal continuity for certain type signs only, especially the simplest ones: the symbol showing a basic trident shape (fig. 2, sign no. 41), the X shape sign, the straight lines (fig. 2, signs no. 20, 21 and 22) and the semicircles (fig. 2, signs no. 1, 2,3, 4 and 5). These signs which occur singly, in pairs or in groups are in some way suggestive of a system of numerical notation employed during the manufacturing cycle. They may represent strokes for counting on, analogous with many known writing systems. Numerals seem to have been expressed in this way in the Indus script. Groups of vertical strokes and semicircles repeated one above another are often depicted on seals. But this resemblance with a numerical system is not really apparent within the complete corpus in which there is a great disproportion of the different marks. Moreover many marks are unique sign types, and many designs seem too complex to have a numerical significance. There is an apparent increase in the number of sign types from Period IV to Period VII B of Mehrgarh and the contemporary Period I B of Nausharo.

Concluding Remarks: Pot Marks and Pottery Technology So far it is difficult to prove what purpose the pot marks served. At best, some interpretations can be eliminated. According to the distribution of the pot marks through time, the marking system was chiefly used at Mehrgarh in Periods VI and VII A-B (beginning of the third millennium). The wide corpus of complete vessels belonging to these periods indicates clearly that there is no link between the marks and the quality or function of the pots. The wide corpus of complete vessels belonging to these periods indicates clearly that there is no link between the marks and the quality or function of the pots. Neither are they indicators of capacity. The large proportion of pots not incised with marks and the study of the ceramic material found in situ in several storage rooms does not suggest concepts such as means of facilitating some kind of registration after firing, or of trademarks, and it does not argue for the possibility that the marks served to identify the individual who owned the pots. The true nature of the marking system was perhaps required not when the pots were in use, but before, during the manufacturing cycle, between the final stage of forming and the moment the vessels stacked in the kiln were removed from it after firing.’ As regards manufacturing, it is interesting to note that the finest examples of the potter’s craft come from those periods whose craftsmen had perfected firing techniques (e.g., the coated jars used as saggars) and decorating techniques (e.g., splendidly decorated Grey Ware). There is a range of remarkable pots beautifully decorated with a vast repertoire of complex painted designs showing the skill of the potters and the particular care involved in their production. During the subsequent Period I C (2700 BC) at Nausharo at the time when the use of incised marks decrease considerably important changes in pottery manufacture are noticed. A new kiln type appears during that period. Many examples were excavated at Lal Shah, a site located near Mehrgarh, where the pottery was similar in all respects to that of Nausharo Period I C (Pracchia 1985). The kilns are double chambered, and in the middle of the combustion chamber stood a column which supported the perforated floor of a firing chamber holding the pots to be fired. The kilns were grouped in rows on two levels. They resemble more recent firing structures of Mohenjo-daro or Harappa as well as kilns uncovered at Nausharo in the mature Indus levels of Period HI. In pottery style, this Period I C is characterized by, for example, the disappearance of Grey Painted

They resemble more recent firing structures of Mohenjo-daro or Harappa as well as kilns uncovered at Nausharo in the mature Indus levels of Period HI. In pottery style, this Period I C is characterized by, for example, the disappearance of Grey Painted Ware and by a predilection for Buff Ware. Several new pot types are then manufactured resembling some of the recorded vessels from later Indus periods. Other proto-Indus elements become characteristic of the pottery, like in painting styles, the intersecting patterns of circles or the black geometrical decoration in red slip painted on the small globular jars similar to pottery found in the transitional layers of Kot-Diji (Quivron 1994). Elaborate painted vases are still manufactured but the vessels have no longer the splendid quality noticed during the previous periods. Contrary also to these previous periods, the bottom of much of the pottery shows specific concentric markings made by the thread used to remove the pots from the wheel indicating the use of a continuously 7 The marks were perhaps used to avoid confusion of ownership during the firing in cases where the vessels were fired in communal kilns. To explain the presence of many pots without marks, may be only the topmost pot of a stack of vessels was marked to distinguish this stack from other identical looking stacks being fired in the same kiln by another potter.

It would be interesting to know if this new dynamic stage of development in the pottery craft activities in Period I C had some implications in the organization of the workshops; and, for example, . to know if the spectacular decrease in the number of pots incised with marks noticed during this period, is linked to these changes or is merely accidental. Seals and Sealings from the Ahar-Banas Culture MARTA AMERI The sites that belong to the Ahar-Banas complex are located primarily in the Mewar region of southwestern Rajasthan, to the east of the Aravalli mountain range, which runs from Gujarat to Delhi and bisects the state diagonally. They cluster around the Banas River and its tributaries, the Ahar, the Berach, the Gambiri, the Kothari and the Khari.' The sites vary in size from a tiny 0.3 hectares (Tarawat) to a fairly substantial 22 ha. (Gilund), but seem to cluster at around five hectares in size. The exploration of the Ahar-Banas Culture began with the excavations at the site of Ahar, in Rajasthan, in 1952, and then again in 1954—55 and 1955-56. These excavations exposed a copper-using, agriculturally-based culture that was defined by a White Painted Black and Red Ware pottery but showed little connection to the Harappan sites found further to the south and west. Surveys conducted in this part of southeastern Rajasthan revealed almost 50 more sites with the typical White Painted Black and Red Ware and a similar subsistence base (Misra 1967: 148). In 1959, Gilund, a second site belonging to the same cultural milieu as Ahar was excavated by B. B. Lal (Ghosh 1960). Excavations at Ahar were eventually resumed by H. D Sankalia in 1962. Most of the sites excavated and surveyed were briefly published in Indian Archaeology — A Review’, but only Ahar was fully published by Sankalia in 1969 (Sankalia et al. 1969). The material from these two sites, Ahar and Gilund, though originally loosely defined and poorly published, served as the basis for the exploration and definition of the AharBanas cultural complex until the 1990s when Deccan College opened up its field school at Balathal (Hooja 1988). Renewed excavations at Gilund in the early 2000s? and the exploration of new sites at Chatrikhera (Raczek et al. 2010) and Pachamta (Raczek et al. 2019) have served to further expand our knowledge of this area. The Chalcolithic period in the Ahar-Banas is generally divided into three phases based on archaeological materials and radiocarbon dates from various sites. The best evidence for the early periods is preserved at Balathal (Mishra 2005), while the layers excavated at Gilund (Shinde et al. 2014) and Ahar (Sankalia et al. 1969)

served to further expand our knowledge of this area. The Chalcolithic period in the Ahar-Banas is generally divided into three phases based on archaeological materials and radiocarbon dates from various sites. The best evidence for the early periods is preserved at Balathal (Mishra 2005), while the layers excavated at Gilund (Shinde et al. 2014) and Ahar (Sankalia et al. 1969) seem to fall into the middle and later periods. The corpus of sealings found at Gilund is made up of 249 fragments of sealing clay, many of which had been impressed by stamp seals. The sealings were found primarily in contexts that can be dated to the Middle Ahar-Banas period. The majority (G.S. 4.001-4.214) of the 249 sealings from Gilund were unearthed during the fourth season (2002-2003). A second, smaller set of sealings (GS 1.001—1.008) was found in a large pit (lot 1014) during the first season of excavation (1999-2000). Other impressions were found singly throughout the excavated areas of GLD-2, but rarely in significant contexts. Most of the sealings found during season 5, for example, were found in contexts that can best be characterized as slope wash. The sealings were not given individual antiquity numbers when they were first excavated, but have since been given GS (Gilund Sealing) numbers. All the sealings found after 2003 were also given GS numbers. The seals from Gilund consist of a set of decorated terracotta objects that may have been used to make impressions on wet clay or other materials. These objects can be divided into two groups: the seal amulets, which are flat and mostly round in shape, and the stamps, which are distinguished by the fact that they have a knob or handle on the undecorated side. Both groups are decorated with carved intaglio designs and vary widely in decoration. The seal amulets and stamps found at Gilund were collected as antiquities and as such were each given an individual antiquity number. The antiquity numbers from Gilund consist of a first number preceded by an S, which denotes the excavation season when an artifact was found, and a second number that gives each object a unique identity. The material found at Balathal included four sealings, one medium jar stopper, two objects that may have functioned as stamp seals, and one small stamped token. A close examination of the contexts in which the seals and sealings were found, both at Gilund and at other Ahar-Banas sites, shows that these materials are part of a tradition that was in existence as early as the Middle Ahar‘Banas period (ca. 2500-2000 BCE) and continued until the end of the Late Ahar-Banas period (2000-1700 BCE). The majority of the sealings from Gilund were found in a pit and a bin associated with the parallel-wall structure. This building is dated to the Middle Ahar-Banas period based on ceramic comparisons to the well-dated material from Balathal. The evidence for at least three reconstructions suggests that this structure was in use for an extended period of time. A further confirmation of the early date for the Gilund sealings is provided by the sealings from Balathal. These sealings were found in Layers 14, 15, and 16, all of which have been firmly dated to the Middle Ahar-Banas period. Published C-14 dates for these layers range from 3130-2750 BCE at the earliest to 2570-1660 BCE at the latest (Mishra 2005). On the other hand, the majority of the terracotta stamps and seal amulets from Gilund were found in habitation contexts at the top of the mound. Most of these have been dated to the Late Ahar-Banas period. Two radiocarbon samples from these uppermost layers of GLD-2 (Area I) give dates of 1630-1440, and 1690-1510 2 cal BCE. This later date for the terracotta stamps and amulets seems to be confirmed by the amulets from Ahar, most of which were also found in later (Ib or Ic) contexts (Deo 1969). The supposition that the sealings and the seals may not be contemporary is also supported by the fact that there is so little overlap in the designs found on the two sets of material. The supposition that the sealings and the seals may not be contemporary is also supported by the fact that there is so little overlap in the designs found on the two sets of material. In addition to the discrepancy in the dating of the seals and the sealings there is also a significant difference in the contexts in which they were found. While the seal amulets and stamps were found primarily in habitation contexts in the uppermost, central part of GLD-2, the sealings were found in features (a pit and a bin) associated with a large structure that was almost definitely public in function. This suggests that seals may have been kept in the home, but were used in areas associated with public structures. Unfortunately, at Gilund there is no physical connection between the houses at the top of the mound and the building with the parallel walls. The sealings from Gilund were first partially published by Possehl, Shinde and Ameri in 2004, and have since been published in full, along with the seals and amulets in Ameri 2014. The seals and sealings from Balathal were not published in any of the publications of the site, but are illustrated and discussed in Ameri 2010 (pp. 138-142, Appendix 1).
